title: Plato's Theory of Immortality
orientation: This chapter examines the Phaedo, Plato's dramatic account of Socrates's last hours and death, and the arguments for the soul's immortality that Plato places in his mouth. Russell treats the Phaedo as ethically pivotal -- 'what the gospel account of the Passion... was for Christians, the Phaedo was for pagan or freethinking philosophers' -- while arguing that the philosophical arguments it offers for immortality are, examined closely, very weak. The chapter closes with Russell's own frank ethical assessment of the Platonic Socrates as a person.
historical_background: Russell situates the Phaedo against the earlier dialogue Crito, in which friends arrange Socrates's escape from prison and he refuses, arguing that having been condemned by due legal process, escape would be an unjust betrayal of the laws of Athens that raised him. Socrates's calm, fearless acceptance of a death sentence he regarded as unjust was, Russell notes, of profound ethical importance both in antiquity and afterward, and its themes of divine justice, bodily imprisonment, and the soul's fate after death fed directly into later Christian theology, 'largely derived from it, directly or indirectly.'
philosophical_problems: Is the soul immortal, and if so, what arguments can establish this?
What is the relationship between soul and body, and does philosophy require withdrawal from bodily concerns?
Can knowledge (especially of a priori truths like exact equality) be explained by the soul's pre-existence?
Is a simple, indivisible thing incapable of dissolution, and does this apply to the soul?
Was Socrates, as Plato portrays him, admirable as a philosopher as well as as a man facing death?

philosophers_discussed.name: Plato
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Primary subject: Russell reconstructs the Phaedo's dramatic frame, Plato's soul/body dualism, his account of the philosophic life as a preparation for death, and the three arguments Plato has Socrates give for immortality (from opposites, from recollection, from simplicity), together with his account of transmigration.

philosophers_discussed.name: Socrates
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: As Plato's dramatized character (Russell repeatedly notes he is 'concerned only with the man as Plato portrays him'): calmly faces execution, refuses to escape, argues for the soul's immortality, and is subjected at the chapter's end to Russell's own mixed ethical verdict.

philosophers_discussed.name: Cebes
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: A companion of Socrates in the Phaedo who voices doubt about the soul's survival after death and prompts Socrates's arguments; later observes that only half the case (pre-existence) has been proven, prompting the argument from simplicity.

philosophers_discussed.name: Simmias
philosophers_discussed.role_in_chapter: Raises the Pythagorean objection that the soul might be merely a 'harmony' of the body, which would not survive the body's destruction; Socrates replies that the soul, unlike a harmony, is simple, not complex.

core_concepts.name: Soul-body dualism
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Plato treats the soul and the body as two fundamentally different things: the soul is akin to the eternal, unchanging Ideas, while the body belongs to the changing, sensible world, and death is simply their separation.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Plato's metaphysical pairing, in the Phaedo, of soul with reality/ideas/reason and body with appearance/sensible-objects/sense-perception, in which the first term of each pair is superior in both reality and goodness to the second, with death defined as the soul's separation from the body.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It grounds both Plato's epistemology (the body is a hindrance to true knowledge) and his ethics (the philosopher should minimize attachment to bodily concerns), and was adopted, in modified form, by Christianity.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Traced by Russell to Orphic religious doctrine, in which the soul is 'the child of earth and of the starry heaven,' the body from earth, the soul from heaven.
examples: 'Death is the separation of soul and body.'
objections: Russell notes Christianity adopted the dualism only in part, blocked by two obstacles Plato's logic does not face: that a good Creator could not have made a body-based world if the body is evil, and that orthodox Christianity, unlike the Manichaeans, could never condemn marriage outright.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Became 'a commonplace in philosophy and science and popular thought' as the mind/matter distinction, per Russell, despite its religious origin.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Rooted in Orphic religious doctrine of the soul's divine origin and the body's earthly origin.

core_concepts.name: Philosophy as preparation for death (moderate asceticism)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: The true philosopher does not fear death but welcomes it, since it frees the soul from the body's distractions; but Plato's ideal philosopher is not a harsh ascetic who struggles against pleasure -- he simply becomes absorbed in higher things and forgets bodily indulgence.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Plato's portrait of the philosophic life as one in which bodily pleasures (food, drink, sex, adornment) are not forbidden by effortful self-denial but are naturally neglected because the philosopher's attention is fixed on the soul and the pursuit of truth, so that the resulting asceticism is 'not, properly speaking, ascetic' in intention.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: Russell uses it to make an important ethical point: bodily pleasure is not the only kind of pleasure, and some of the worst human vices (love of power, cruelty, envy) are purely mental, so indifference to bodily pleasure does not by itself guarantee virtue.
examples: Socrates, though indifferent to wine, could out-drink anyone without becoming intoxicated -- it was not drinking he condemned, but pleasure in drinking.
Russell's own observation: 'I have known many philosophers who forgot their meals, and read a book when at last they did eat.'
objections: Russell: this view, popularized, becomes genuinely ascetic and can mislead moralists into thinking anyone who avoids bodily pleasure must be virtuous -- but 'the worst pleasures, as well as the best, are mental,' citing envy, cruelty, and love of power (with Hitler given as a contemporary example).
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: Russell connects the mistaken popularized version to real historical harm done by ecclesiastics who, having renounced bodily pleasure, became dominated by unchecked love of power.
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Echoes Orphic notions of ritual 'purity,' reinterpreted by Plato as freedom from bodily slavery.

core_concepts.name: The theory of recollection (anamnesis)
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Plato argues that because we have ideas -- like 'exact equality' -- that we could never have gotten purely from imperfect sense experience, we must have known them before birth and simply be 'remembering' them; this is meant to prove the soul existed before the body.
core_concepts.precise_definition: The doctrine that all a priori knowledge (especially mathematical and logical concepts such as absolute equality, which is never actually found among sensible objects) is recollection of knowledge the soul possessed in a prior, disembodied existence, developed in the Phaedo and at greater length in the Meno via the interrogation of an untutored slave-boy about geometry.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It is Plato's central argument for the soul's pre-existence (half of the case for full immortality), and it later shaped rationalist views of innate ideas.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Presented in the Phaedo and elaborated in the Meno ('there is no teaching, but only recollection').
examples: We experience only approximate equality among sensible things, yet we understand 'absolute equality' -- which, Plato argues, we must have brought with us from a prior existence.
The Meno's slave-boy, questioned by Socrates about geometry, appears to 'remember' truths he was never taught.
objections: Russell: the argument is wholly inapplicable to empirical knowledge (the slave-boy could not 'remember' historical facts like the building of the Pyramids unless he had actually been present); Russell also doubts we truly possess an idea of 'absolute equality' at all, given that even the best modern measurement of a metre rod yields only an empirical, revisable claim, not certainty.

Even granting the idea exists, it is 'elicited by experience, although not directly derived from it,' and children do not possess it until a certain age; and if it were explained by a prior existence, the same problem simply recurs one step back, since that prior existence would need its own source for the idea.
core_concepts.influence_on_later_thinkers: A forerunner of later rationalist doctrines of innate ideas.

core_concepts.name: The argument from simplicity
core_concepts.plain_explanation: Only things made of parts can be broken apart and destroyed; the soul, like the eternal Ideas it contemplates, is simple (not made of parts), so it cannot be dissolved and must be indestructible.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Plato's argument that dissolution presupposes composition, that the soul (unlike the body) is simple and akin in nature to the unchanging essences it is capable of contemplating, and therefore, like those essences, cannot begin, end, or change -- and so must be classified among eternal things.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It supplies the second half of Plato's case for immortality (survival after death, as recollection supplied survival before birth), and provoked the influential Pythagorean counter-objection that the soul might be a mere 'harmony' of the body.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Developed in response to Cebes's observation that pre-existence alone does not establish post-mortem survival.
examples: Absolute beauty is always the same, while beautiful things continually change; the soul, being eternal, 'is at home' contemplating unchanging essences but becomes confused when it engages with the changing sensible world.
objections: Simmias's Pythagorean objection: if the soul is like a harmony produced by a lyre's strings, it cannot survive the lyre's destruction. Socrates replies that a harmony is complex while the soul is simple, and that the harmony view is incompatible with the already-established pre-existence of the soul, since a harmony cannot exist before the instrument that produces it.
competing_positions: Simmias's harmony theory of the soul, ultimately rejected within the dialogue.

core_concepts.name: Transmigration and the fate of souls
core_concepts.plain_explanation: After death, the philosopher's purified soul goes to live in bliss with the gods, while lesser souls are reborn as animals fitting their character -- cowardly or unrighteous men become asses, wolves, or hawks, while merely virtuous non-philosophers become social insects like bees.
core_concepts.precise_definition: Plato's account of post-mortem judgment in which the truly philosophic soul, liberated in life from bodily 'thraldom,' departs to the invisible world to dwell with the gods, while impure souls either haunt sepulchres as ghosts or are reborn into animal bodies suited to their moral character.
core_concepts.why_it_mattered: It supplies the practical, ethical payoff of the whole theory: only philosophy secures the best afterlife, which is Plato's stated reason for the philosopher's ascetic self-discipline.
core_concepts.historical_origin: Drawn from Orphic and Pythagorean doctrines of the soul's transmigration.
examples: 'No one who has not studied philosophy and who is not entirely pure at the time of his departure is allowed to enter the company of the Gods, but the lover of knowledge only.'
core_concepts.connection_to_politics_or_religion: Directly continuous with Orphic religious eschatology.

arguments.title: The argument from generation of opposites
premises: All things that have opposites are generated from their opposites.
arguments.conclusion: Death must generate life just as life generates death, so the souls of the dead must exist somewhere and eventually return to earth.
arguments.explanation: Russell notes this recalls Anaximander's views on cosmic justice, and links it to Saint Paul's statement 'the seed is not quickened except it die.' Russell says plainly that, of the Phaedo's arguments for immortality, 'it must be said that the arguments are very poor,' and this is the weakest of the three.
objections: Not developed in detail by Russell, beyond noting the argument's poor overall quality.
implications: Provides only the weakest support for the doctrine, later supplemented by the stronger-seeming (but still, per Russell, flawed) recollection and simplicity arguments.

arguments.title: The argument from recollection
premises: We possess ideas, such as exact equality, that are not derivable from ordinary sense experience of only approximately equal things.
Such ideas must therefore have been acquired before birth.
arguments.conclusion: The soul existed, with knowledge, before its present bodily existence -- 'about half' of the case for full immortality (pre-existence, not yet post-mortem survival).
arguments.explanation: Developed in the Phaedo and at greater length in the Meno's slave-boy demonstration. Russell walks through why the argument seems initially plausible for a priori knowledge (logic and mathematics) even though it plainly fails for empirical knowledge (history, geography).
objections: The argument is wholly inapplicable to empirical knowledge.
Russell doubts we possess a genuine idea of 'absolute equality' at all -- even the most precise physical measurement yields only an empirical, revisable claim.
Even granting the idea exists, it is elicited by, though not directly derived from, experience, and children acquire it only at a certain age.
If a prior existence explains the idea, and that prior existence was itself sense-based, the same explanatory gap simply recurs one step earlier.
implications: If the argument fails, as Russell argues, Plato's positive case for the soul's pre-existence collapses, undermining half the total case for immortality.

arguments.title: The argument from the soul's simplicity
premises: Only what is complex (composed of parts) can be dissolved.
The soul, like the eternal essences it can contemplate, is simple, not compounded of parts.
What is simple cannot begin, end, or change.
arguments.conclusion: The soul, being simple and akin to the eternal, unchanging essences, belongs to the class of eternal things and so survives the body's destruction.
arguments.explanation: This supplies the second half of the case Cebes demands: not just pre-existence, but survival after death. Socrates supports it by noting the soul's affinity with the unchanging Ideas it is uniquely capable of knowing, in contrast to its 'drunken,' confused state when engaged with the changing sensible world.
objections: Simmias raises the Pythagorean 'harmony' objection: the soul may be like the harmony produced by a lyre, which does not survive the lyre's destruction. Socrates replies that harmony is complex (so the analogy fails, since the soul is claimed to be simple) and that harmony cannot pre-exist its instrument, contradicting the already-established doctrine of pre-existence.
implications: If sound, it would establish full immortality (both pre-existence and post-mortem survival); Russell does not explicitly refute this argument as he does the recollection argument, but groups it among the Phaedo's generally 'very poor' arguments.

key_distinctions: Soul (akin to Ideas, reason, reality) vs. body (akin to sense-perception, appearance)
Genuine philosophic indifference to bodily pleasure vs. effortful, popularized asceticism
Bodily pleasures/vices vs. purely mental pleasures/vices (e.g., cruelty, love of power)
Pre-existence of the soul (established, in Plato's view, by recollection) vs. post-mortem survival (requiring the further argument from simplicity)
The fate of the philosophic soul (bliss with the gods) vs. the fate of the merely virtuous or vicious soul (transmigration into humans or animals)
connections_to_earlier_philosophers: Russell traces the soul/body dualism and the doctrine of purification to Orphic religion, the argument from opposites to a pattern of thought resembling Anaximander's cosmic justice, and the harmony theory of the soul (raised by Simmias) to Pythagorean doctrine. He also connects the recollection argument to the broader Pythagorean-Orphic theme of the soul's pre-existence and transmigration.
connections_to_later_philosophers: Russell draws an extended parallel between the Phaedo and the Christian gospel account of the Passion, and states that 'the theology of St. Paul and of the Fathers was largely derived from it, directly or indirectly.' He quotes Saint Paul's 'the seed is not quickened except it die' alongside the argument from opposites, and compares Plato's claim that wars are caused by love of money to Marx's materialist view of the causes of war (while noting Plato's very different conclusion about the remedy). Russell also cites Hitler as a modern instance of Plato's warning that indifference to bodily pleasure can coexist with -- or even enable -- a ruinous love of power.
political_social_context: Russell observes that a philosopher's exemption from bodily labor, which Plato takes for granted, in fact depends on economic conditions: 'It was the imperialism of Athens in the age of Pericles that made it possible for Athenians to study philosophy,' since intellectual goods, like material ones, require the labor of others to sustain them (libraries, leisure, and so on).
religion_science_culture_context: The whole chapter is steeped in Orphic and Pythagorean religious vocabulary -- 'purity,' 'mysteries,' 'initiation' -- which Plato repurposes as philosophical terms for freedom from bodily slavery; Russell notes this mystical language is 'derived from the mysteries' even as it does genuine philosophical work in the dialogue.
russell_presentation: Russell first sets the Phaedo's dramatic scene via the earlier Crito (Socrates's refusal to escape execution, on the ground that legal condemnation must be honored even when unjust) and then the Phaedo itself: the calm final hours, the argument against suicide (man as a 'prisoner' who may not free himself before God summons him), the definition of death as separation of soul and body, and the resulting moderate asceticism, whose genuine and popularized (mis)readings Russell carefully distinguishes. He then presents the 'intellectual aspect' of the doctrine -- the claim that true knowledge requires abandoning sense-perception entirely, which Russell notes 'involves a complete rejection of empirical knowledge, including all history and geography' -- before walking through Plato's three arguments for immortality (from opposites, from recollection, from simplicity) in the order the dialogue gives them, including Cebes's and Simmias's objections. He closes with the dialogue's famous final scene (Socrates's request to pay a cock to Asclepius) and Phaedo's verdict that Socrates was 'the wisest and justest and best' of his time.
critical_context: Russell states plainly that, of the arguments the Phaedo offers for immortality, 'it must be said that the arguments are very poor,' and he mounts a detailed rebuttal of the recollection argument specifically (its inapplicability to empirical knowledge, doubt about whether we truly possess an idea of 'absolute equality,' and the regress problem if pre-existence is invoked to explain it). He closes the chapter with his own, separately flagged ethical assessment of the Platonic Socrates as a person: admiring his indifference to worldly success and his fearless calm, but judging him 'dishonest and sophistical in argument,' using intellect to reach conclusions he found agreeable rather than in disinterested search of truth -- 'this is treachery to truth, and the worst of philosophic sins' -- and noting that his courage would be 'more remarkable if he had not believed he was going to enjoy eternal bliss in the company of the gods.' Russell explicitly separates the ethical verdict on Socrates 'the man' from the harsher philosophical verdict on Socrates 'the philosopher.'
key_takeaways: The Phaedo dramatizes Socrates's last hours and death, and was, for later pagan and Christian readers alike, comparable in importance to the gospel Passion narrative.
Plato's soul/body dualism (soul akin to reason, Ideas, and reality; body akin to sense, appearance, and change) underlies both his epistemology and his ethics of moderate, non-effortful asceticism.

Plato gives three arguments for immortality -- from the generation of opposites, from recollection (anamnesis), and from the soul's simplicity -- which Russell judges collectively weak, singling out the recollection argument for detailed refutation.

The theory of recollection holds that a priori ideas like 'absolute equality,' not derivable from sense experience, prove the soul knew them in a prior existence; Russell doubts both that we possess such an idea and that the argument, even granted, proves anything beyond mere age-dependent development.
Simmias's Pythagorean 'harmony' objection -- that the soul might be like a harmony that cannot outlive its instrument -- is answered by Socrates's claim that the soul, unlike a harmony, is simple.
Russell separates his admiration for Socrates as a man facing death from his sharply critical judgment of Socrates as a philosopher, whom he accuses of 'treachery to truth.'
study_notes:
Read this chapter on two levels at once, as with the previous one: first the internal structure of Plato's argument, then Russell's running and closing critique. Internally, notice that Plato structures the case for immortality in two explicit stages, matching Cebes's own framing: first prove the soul existed before birth (the recollection argument), then prove it survives after death (the simplicity argument, defended against Simmias's harmony objection). Keeping this two-part structure in mind makes the sequence of arguments much easier to follow.

Pay special attention to Russell's treatment of the recollection argument, since it is his most detailed piece of critical analysis in the chapter. His key move is to distinguish sharply between a priori knowledge (logic, mathematics) and empirical knowledge (history, geography): the recollection theory might have some initial plausibility for the former but is obviously absurd for the latter (a slave-boy cannot 'remember' when the Pyramids were built). He then goes further and questions whether we really have the very idea -- 'absolute equality' -- that the argument depends on, using the modern example of the standard metre to suggest that even our most precise physical claims remain empirical and revisable rather than the product of some perfect, remembered Idea.

Finally, do not skip the closing few paragraphs, where Russell steps back from exposition of doctrine to render a personal ethical verdict on Socrates. This is one of the more striking moments in the book: Russell openly separates 'the man' (admirable in his fearlessness and indifference to worldly success) from 'the philosopher' (whom he accuses of using argument dishonestly, to reach conclusions he wanted rather than the truth). This closing judgment sets up Russell's continuing, often skeptical treatment of Plato's legacy in the following chapters.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that the soul and body are two completely different kinds of thing, with the soul being the higher, more real of the two.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Plato's metaphysical pairing of soul with reason/Ideas/reality and body with sense-perception/appearance/change, with death defined as their separation.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Plato's idea that learning is really just 'remembering' knowledge the soul had before it was born.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The doctrine that a priori knowledge, especially mathematical and logical concepts not derivable from sense experience, is recollected from a prior, disembodied existence of the soul.

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The claim that because the soul has no parts, it can't be broken apart or destroyed the way composite things can.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: Plato's argument that dissolution presupposes composition, that the soul is simple and akin to the unchanging essences it contemplates, and is therefore indestructible.
related_concepts: The argument from the soul's simplicity

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: Simmias's Pythagorean-inspired suggestion that the soul might just be like the 'tune' produced by the body, which can't outlive the instrument.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The objection, raised by Simmias, that the soul is analogous to the harmony (attunement) produced by a lyre's strings, and so cannot survive the destruction of the body that produces it; rejected by Socrates on the grounds that a harmony is complex while the soul is simple.
related_concepts: The argument from the soul's simplicity

glossary_terms.beginner_explanation: The idea that after death, souls are reborn into new bodies -- human or animal -- depending on how they lived.
glossary_terms.academic_explanation: The Orphic-Pythagorean doctrine, adopted by Plato, that impure or merely virtuous (non-philosophic) souls are reborn into human or animal bodies fitting their moral character, while purified philosophic souls dwell with the gods.
related_concepts: Transmigration and the fate of souls

questions.prompt: Why does Socrates, in the Crito, refuse the opportunity to escape execution?
questions.answer: He argues that he was condemned through due legal process, that it would be wrong to act illegally to avoid punishment, and that he owes the laws of Athens the respect a son owes a father, having freely chosen to remain a citizen.
questions.explanation: This establishes the ethical seriousness with which Plato frames Socrates's death well before the Phaedo's arguments for immortality begin.

questions.prompt: How does Plato define death, and what dualism does this definition rest on?
questions.answer: Death is defined as the separation of soul and body, resting on Plato's dualism between soul (akin to reason, Ideas, reality) and body (akin to sense-perception, appearance, change).
questions.explanation: This dualism underlies the rest of the chapter's arguments.

questions.prompt: Contrast genuine Platonic philosophic 'indifference' to bodily pleasure with the popularized, effortful asceticism Russell warns against.
questions.answer: Plato's philosopher does not struggle against bodily pleasure through moral effort; he is simply absorbed in higher pursuits and neglects it naturally. The popularized, effortful version wrongly assumes that avoiding bodily pleasure by itself guarantees virtue, ignoring that purely mental vices like cruelty and love of power can be just as serious.
questions.explanation: Russell uses Hitler as a contemporary example of someone indifferent to bodily pleasure who was nonetheless dominated by love of power.

questions.prompt: Reconstruct the theory-of-recollection argument for the soul's pre-existence, and give Russell's main objection to it.
questions.answer: We possess ideas, like exact equality, not derivable from sense experience of only approximately equal things; therefore we must have acquired such ideas before birth, proving the soul's pre-existence. Russell objects that the argument is inapplicable to empirical knowledge, that we may not even possess a genuine idea of absolute equality, and that even if we do, invoking a prior existence only pushes the same explanatory problem back a step.
questions.explanation: This argument supplies only 'half' of Plato's case for immortality, per Cebes.

questions.prompt: What objection does Simmias raise against the argument from the soul's simplicity, and how does Socrates answer it?
questions.answer: Simmias suggests the soul might be like a harmony produced by a lyre, which cannot outlive the lyre. Socrates replies that a harmony is complex, whereas the soul is simple, and that the harmony theory is incompatible with the soul's already-established pre-existence, since a harmony cannot exist before its instrument.
questions.explanation: This is the dialogue's most serious internal challenge to the immortality arguments.

questions.prompt: According to Russell, what economic condition made it possible for Athenians to pursue philosophy in Plato's sense?
questions.answer: The imperialism of Athens under Pericles, which generated the wealth needed to support philosophers who did not engage in manual labor, since intellectual goods, like material ones, depend on economic conditions.
questions.explanation: Russell uses this to puncture Plato's suggestion that philosophy requires only minimal material needs.

questions.prompt: Summarize Russell's final ethical assessment of the Platonic Socrates, distinguishing his judgment of Socrates as a man from his judgment of Socrates as a philosopher.
questions.answer: As a man, Russell admires Socrates's indifference to worldly success and his calm, fearless acceptance of death. As a philosopher, Russell judges him 'dishonest and sophistical in argument,' using intellect to prove conclusions agreeable to him rather than in disinterested search of truth -- 'treachery to truth, and the worst of philosophic sins.'
questions.explanation: Russell explicitly separates these two verdicts rather than blending them into one overall judgment.

flashcards.front: What earlier dialogue describes Socrates's refusal to escape execution, and why does he refuse?
flashcards.back: The Crito; he argues that lawful condemnation must be honored, since escaping would wrong the laws of Athens that raised and protected him.

flashcards.front: How does Plato define death in the Phaedo?
flashcards.back: As the separation of soul and body.

flashcards.front: What does Plato say is the source of the soul/body distinction, per Russell?
flashcards.back: Orphic religious doctrine: the soul comes from heaven, the body from earth.

flashcards.front: Is Plato's ideal philosophic 'asceticism' the result of moral effort, according to the chapter?
flashcards.back: No -- properly speaking it is not effortful asceticism; the philosopher simply becomes absorbed in higher pursuits and neglects bodily pleasure naturally.

flashcards.front: What three arguments does Plato give in the Phaedo for the soul's immortality?
flashcards.back: The argument from the generation of opposites, the argument from recollection (anamnesis), and the argument from the soul's simplicity.

flashcards.front: What example does Plato use to support the theory of recollection in the Meno?
flashcards.back: Socrates questions an untutored slave-boy about geometry, and the boy appears to 'remember' truths he was never taught.

flashcards.front: What is Russell's chief objection to the recollection argument?
flashcards.back: It is inapplicable to empirical knowledge (history, geography), and Russell doubts we even possess a true idea of 'absolute equality' that could require a prior existence to explain.

flashcards.front: What Pythagorean objection does Simmias raise against the soul's immortality?
flashcards.back: That the soul might be merely a 'harmony' produced by the body, like the tune of a lyre, which cannot survive the lyre's destruction.

flashcards.front: How does Socrates answer Simmias's harmony objection?
flashcards.back: A harmony is complex, but the soul is simple; also, a harmony cannot exist before its instrument, contradicting the soul's already-established pre-existence.

flashcards.front: According to Plato, what happens to the soul of a true philosopher after death?
flashcards.back: It departs, liberated from bodily 'thraldom,' to live in bliss with the gods.

flashcards.front: What comparison does Russell draw between Plato's claim that wars are caused by love of money and a later thinker?
flashcards.back: He compares it to Marx's view that wars are caused by economic/material interests, while noting the two thinkers draw very different practical conclusions.

flashcards.front: What economic point does Russell make about philosophy's material requirements?
flashcards.back: Intellectual goods, like material goods, are expensive and dependent on economic conditions -- Athenian imperialism under Pericles made philosophy possible.

flashcards.front: What are Socrates's last words in the Phaedo?
flashcards.back: 'Crito, I owe a cock to Asclepius; will you remember to pay the debt?'

flashcards.front: What is Russell's overall verdict on Socrates as a philosopher (as opposed to as a man)?
flashcards.back: He judges him dishonest and sophistical in argument, using intellect to reach conclusions he found agreeable rather than pursuing truth disinterestedly -- 'treachery to truth.'

quiz.prompt: In the Crito, why does Socrates refuse the chance to escape execution?
options: He fears being caught
He believes escaping would wrongly break faith with the laws of Athens that raised him
He wants to become a martyr for fame
He does not believe he will actually be executed
quiz.explanation: Socrates argues that lawful condemnation, even if unjust, must be respected rather than evaded illegally.

quiz.prompt: Plato's ideal philosopher achieves indifference to bodily pleasure mainly through deliberate, effortful self-denial.
options: True
False
quiz.explanation: Russell stresses that, in Plato's portrayal, the philosopher's indifference arises naturally from absorption in higher pursuits, not effortful denial.
quiz.related_concept: Philosophy as preparation for death (moderate asceticism)

quiz.prompt: What are the three arguments for immortality Plato gives in the Phaedo?
options: From design, from motion, from causation
From opposites, from recollection, from simplicity
From pleasure, from pain, from virtue
From dreams, from memory, from prophecy
quiz.explanation: These are the three arguments Russell walks through in sequence.

quiz.prompt: Plato's theory that knowledge is really ___ of what the soul knew before birth is called anamnesis.
options: invention
recollection
imitation
revelation

quiz.prompt: What is Russell's main objection to the recollection argument?
options: It proves too much, showing animals also have souls
It is inapplicable to empirical knowledge, and Russell doubts we truly possess the idea of 'absolute equality' it relies on
It contradicts Plato's earlier theory of the Good
It was disproven by Aristotle's Physics
quiz.explanation: Russell notes the slave-boy could not 'remember' historical facts, and questions whether we really have a precise notion of exact equality at all.

quiz.prompt: What objection does Simmias raise against the soul's immortality?
options: That the soul is identical to the body
That the soul might be a 'harmony' of the body, unable to outlive it
That souls cannot be simple
That immortality is contradicted by transmigration
quiz.explanation: This is the Pythagorean-inspired harmony objection.
quiz.related_concept: The argument from the soul's simplicity

quiz.prompt: According to Plato's account of transmigration, a merely virtuous but non-philosophic person may be reborn as a social insect such as a bee.
options: True
